title: Die Boten des Todes
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 177. Text from Wikisource („Die Boten des Todes (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: Death, here a character who walks the roads like anyone else, is beaten unconscious by a giant and later confronts a man who thought he had escaped him. Death lists the warnings he had already sent — fever, dizziness, gout, toothache, the heaviness of sleep itself — each one a messenger the man failed to read. It is one of Grimm's small allegorical fables rather than a fairy tale proper, closer in spirit to Aesop.

sentences.t: Vor alten Zeiten wanderte einmal ein Riese auf der großen Landstraße, da sprang ihm plötzlich ein unbekannter Mann entgegen und rief „halt! keinen Schritt weiter!“
sentences.l: In old times a giant was once walking on the great highroad, when suddenly an unknown man sprang out to meet him and cried “stop! not a step further!”
sentences.i: In olden times a giant was once walking along the great highroad, when suddenly an unknown man sprang into his path and cried: “Halt! Not a step further!”
sentences.n: vor alten Zeiten is this tale’s way of saying long ago; it opens in a higher register than most of the collection and keeps it to the end. entgegenspringen, to spring toward somebody, takes the dative — ihm, at him. keinen Schritt weiter is a bare accusative with no verb at all: not a step further.

sentences.t: „Was,“ sprach der Riese, „du Wicht, den ich zwischen den Fingern zerdrücken kann, du willst mir den Weg vertreten? Wer bist du, daß du so keck reden darfst?“
sentences.l: “What,” said the giant, “you wretch, whom I can crush between my fingers, you want to bar my way? Who are you, that you dare speak so boldly?”
sentences.i: “What,” said the giant, “you little wretch, whom I could crush between my fingers — you mean to bar my way? Who are you, that you dare to speak so boldly?”
sentences.n: einem den Weg vertreten is to bar or block a man’s way; vertreten here has nothing to do with representing. Wicht is a wretch, a poor small creature — the same word as the old English “wight”. keck is bold to the edge of impudence.

sentences.t: „Ich bin der Tod,“ erwiederte der andere, „mir widersteht niemand, und auch du mußt meinen Befehlen gehorchen.“
sentences.l: “I am Death,” answered the other, “no one withstands me, and you too must obey my commands.”
sentences.n: erwiederte is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte. Both widerstehen and gehorchen take the dative — mir widersteht niemand, meinen Befehlen gehorchen — so what is resisted or obeyed is not a direct object in German at all. Befehlen here is the plural noun Befehle, orders, and not the verb befehlen.

sentences.t: Der Riese aber weigerte sich und fieng an mit dem Tode zu ringen.
sentences.l: But the giant refused and began to wrestle with Death.
sentences.n: fieng … an is anfangen, to begin, with its particle at the end of the clause; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. ringen here is the verb, to wrestle, not a plural of der Ring. dem Tode carries the old dative -e, which this tale uses more than once.

sentences.t: Es war ein langer heftiger Kampf, zuletzt behielt der Riese die Oberhand und schlug den Tod mit seiner Faust nieder, daß er neben einen Stein zusammensank.
sentences.l: It was a long fierce fight; at last the giant kept the upper hand and struck Death down with his fist, so that he sank together beside a stone.
sentences.i: It was a long, fierce fight; at last the giant got the upper hand and struck Death down with his fist, so that he collapsed beside a stone.
sentences.n: die Oberhand behalten, to keep the upper hand. niederschlagen, to strike down, with nieder waiting at the end. daß after a clause like this means so that, giving the result, rather than that.

sentences.t: Der Riese gieng seiner Wege, und der Tod lag da besiegt und war so kraftlos, daß er sich nicht wieder erheben konnte.
sentences.l: The giant went his ways, and Death lay there defeated and was so strengthless that he could not raise himself again.
sentences.i: The giant went on his way, and Death lay there defeated, so powerless that he could not raise himself again.
sentences.n: seiner Wege gehen is a fixed genitive phrase — to go one’s way — and stays plural in German where English turns it singular. sich erheben, to raise oneself, to get up.

sentences.t: „Was soll daraus werden,“ sprach er, „wenn ich da in der Ecke liegen bleibe? es stirbt niemand mehr auf der Welt, und sie wird so mit Menschen angefüllt werden, daß sie nicht mehr Platz haben neben einander zu stehen.“
sentences.l: “What is to come of it,” he said, “if I stay lying here in the corner? nobody dies any more in the world, and it will be so filled up with people that they will no longer have room to stand beside one another.”
sentences.i: “What is to become of this,” he said, “if I lie here in the corner? Nobody in the world will die any more, and it will be so filled with people that they will have no room left to stand side by side.”
sentences.n: was soll daraus werden is the standing German question: what is to come of it. liegen bleiben, to remain lying. es stirbt niemand puts a placeholder es in front and the real subject after the verb — a shape German uses to hold the news back a moment.

sentences.t: Indem kam ein junger Mensch des Wegs, frisch und gesund, sang ein Lied und warf seine Augen hin und her.
sentences.l: Just then a young man came along the way, fresh and healthy, sang a song and threw his eyes here and there.
sentences.i: Just then a young fellow came along the road, fresh and in good health, singing a song and casting his eyes this way and that.
sentences.n: indem here is not “in that” but just then, at that moment — an older use. des Wegs kommen is a genitive of place, to come along the way. Mensch is simply a person; the tale calls him der Jüngling and der Mensch by turns, and it is der Mensch he has become when Death comes for him.

sentences.t: Als er den halbohnmächtigen erblickte, gieng er mitleidig heran, richtete ihn auf, flößte ihm aus seiner Flasche einen stärkenden Trank ein und wartete bis er wieder zu Kräften kam.
sentences.l: When he caught sight of the half-fainting man, he went up compassionately, raised him up, poured him a strengthening draught from his bottle and waited until he came to his strength again.
sentences.i: When he caught sight of the half-fainting man he came up in pity, raised him, poured him a strengthening draught out of his bottle, and waited until his strength came back.
sentences.n: den halbohnmächtigen is an adjective used as a noun, and the 1857 text prints it with a small letter: the half-unconscious one. einflößen is to pour a drink into somebody and aufrichten to set him upright; both split, and their particles ein and auf stand at the ends of their clauses. zu Kräften kommen, to come to one’s strength.

sentences.t: „Weißt du auch,“ fragte der Fremde, indem er sich aufrichtete, „wer ich bin, und wem du wieder auf die Beine geholfen hast?“
sentences.l: “Do you know, then,” asked the stranger, as he raised himself up, “who I am, and whom you have helped back onto his legs?”
sentences.i: “Do you know, then,” asked the stranger, raising himself up, “who I am, and whom you have helped back onto his feet?”
sentences.n: der Fremde is the stranger, another adjective turned into a noun. indem in this sentence does mean while, as — the older sense and the newer one stand two lines apart. helfen takes the dative: wem du geholfen hast, whom you have helped.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Jüngling, „ich kenne dich nicht.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the young man, “I do not know you.”
sentences.n: kennen is to know a person, by sight or acquaintance, where wissen is to know a fact; the tale uses both within a few lines, and English has only the one verb.

sentences.t: „Ich bin der Tod,“ sprach er, „ich verschone niemand und kann auch mit dir keine Ausnahme machen.
sentences.l: “I am Death,” he said, “I spare nobody and can make no exception with you either.
sentences.n: verschone is the plain first person present, I spare, and not an imperative. eine Ausnahme machen, to make an exception.

sentences.t: Damit du aber siehst daß ich dankbar bin, so verspreche ich dir daß ich dich nicht unversehens überfallen sondern dir erst meine Boten senden will, bevor ich komme und dich abhole.“
sentences.l: But so that you see that I am grateful, I promise you that I will not fall upon you unawares but will first send you my messengers, before I come and fetch you away.”
sentences.i: But so that you may see that I am grateful, I promise you this: I shall not fall upon you unawares, but shall first send you my messengers, before I come and fetch you away.”
sentences.n: This promise is the tale, and its exact words are what Death will hold him to at the end. unversehens is unawares, without warning. A single will at the close governs both halves — überfallen … sondern … senden will — so German can hold the modal back to the very end where English has to repeat it. abholen is to come and fetch somebody away.

sentences.t: „Wohlan,“ sprach der Jüngling, „immer ein Gewinn, daß ich weiß wann du kommst und so lange wenigstens sicher vor dir bin.“
sentences.l: “Very well,” said the young man, “always a gain, that I know when you are coming and so long at least am safe from you.”
sentences.i: “Very well,” said the young man, “that is something gained: I shall know when you are coming, and till then at least be safe from you.”
sentences.n: wohlan is an old word of assent, very well then. immer ein Gewinn stands with no verb at all — always a gain — and the English has to supply one. sicher vor is safe from.

sentences.t: Dann zog er weiter, war lustig und guter Dinge und lebte in den Tag hinein.
sentences.l: Then he went on further, was merry and of good cheer and lived into the day.
sentences.i: Then he went on his way, merry and in good spirits, and lived from one day to the next without a thought.
sentences.n: guter Dinge sein is a fixed genitive phrase, to be in good spirits. in den Tag hinein leben is to live with no thought for tomorrow — literally to live into the day; the rest of the tale is an answer to that phrase.

sentences.t: Allein Jugend und Gesundheit hielten nicht lange aus, bald kamen Krankheiten und Schmerzen, die ihn bei Tag plagten und ihm Nachts die Ruhe wegnahmen.
sentences.l: But youth and health did not hold out long; soon came illnesses and pains that plagued him by day and took his rest from him by night.
sentences.i: But youth and health did not hold out long: soon came illnesses and pains that plagued him by day and took away his rest at night.
sentences.n: allein at the head of a sentence is not “alone” but the older conjunction, but, however. aushalten, to hold out, endure, with aus at the end. ihm … die Ruhe wegnahmen is a dative of possession: took the rest from him, where English says his rest.

sentences.t: „Sterben werde ich nicht,“ sprach er zu sich selbst, „denn der Tod sendet erst seine Boten, ich wollte nur die bösen Tage der Krankheit wären erst vorüber.“
sentences.l: “Die I shall not,” he said to himself, “for Death sends his messengers first; I only wish the bad days of the sickness were but over.”
sentences.i: “I shall not die,” he said to himself, “for Death sends his messengers first — I only wish the evil days of this sickness were behind me.”
sentences.n: The infinitive Sterben is pushed to the front of the clause for emphasis, and the literal line keeps it there. ich wollte with a subjunctive is a wish: I only wish; wären is that subjunctive, were. He is quoting the promise back at himself, and reading it wrong.

sentences.t: Sobald er sich gesund fühlte, fieng er wieder an in Freuden zu leben.
sentences.l: As soon as he felt himself healthy, he began again to live in pleasures.
sentences.i: As soon as he felt well again, he set about living in pleasure once more.
sentences.n: sich gesund fühlen — German keeps the reflexive where English drops it: to feel oneself well. in Freuden leben is a set phrase and stays plural, to live in pleasures.

sentences.t: Da klopfte ihn eines Tags jemand auf die Schulter: er blickte sich um, und der Tod stand hinter ihm und sprach „folge mir, die Stunde deines Abschieds von der Welt ist gekommen.“
sentences.l: Then one day somebody tapped him on the shoulder: he looked round, and Death stood behind him and said “follow me, the hour of your parting from the world has come.”
sentences.i: Then one day somebody tapped him on the shoulder: he looked round, and Death was standing behind him, and said: “Follow me — the hour of your parting from the world has come.”
sentences.n: eines Tags is the genitive of time, one day. klopfte ihn … auf die Schulter is the dative-of-possession pattern once more, with the body part taking a plain article instead of a possessive. folgen takes the dative: folge mir.

sentences.t: „Wie,“ antwortete der Mensch, „willst du dein Wort brechen? hast du mir nicht versprochen daß du mir, bevor du selbst kämest, deine Boten senden wolltest? ich habe keinen gesehen.“
sentences.l: “What,” answered the man, “will you break your word? did you not promise me that, before you came yourself, you would send me your messengers? I have seen none.”
sentences.i: “What,” answered the man, “will you break your word? Did you not promise me that before you came yourself you would send me your messengers? I have seen none of them.”
sentences.n: kämest is the past subjunctive of kommen inside reported speech: before you should come; wolltest is the same, you would send. German marks a reported promise as subjunctive from end to end, so the reader can hear that these are the man’s words about Death’s words.

sentences.t: „Schweig,“ erwiederte der Tod, „habe ich dir nicht einen Boten über den andern geschickt?
sentences.l: “Be silent,” answered Death, “have I not sent you one messenger over the other?
sentences.i: “Silence,” answered Death, “have I not sent you one messenger after another?
sentences.n: einen über den andern is one after another, one on top of the last. What follows is a list, and the point of the whole tale is that the reader has been reading that list as illness and not as messengers.

sentences.t: kam nicht das Fieber, stieß dich an, rüttelte dich und warf dich nieder?
sentences.l: did not the fever come, knock against you, shake you and throw you down?
sentences.i: Did the fever not come, strike you, shake you and throw you down?
sentences.n: The messengers are named one by one from here to the end, and every one of them is a plain illness. anstoßen, to knock against, and niederwerfen, to throw down, both split — stieß … an, warf … nieder.

sentences.t: hat der Schwindel dir nicht den Kopf betäubt? zwickte dich nicht die Gicht in allen Gliedern?
sentences.l: has the dizziness not numbed your head? did the gout not pinch you in every limb?
sentences.i: Did the dizziness not make your head swim? Did the gout not pinch you in every limb?
sentences.n: dir … den Kopf is the dative of possession again: your head. Schwindel is giddiness and Gicht is gout; in allen Gliedern, in every limb, is the fixed phrase for an ache that is everywhere at once.

sentences.t: brauste dirs nicht in den Ohren? nagte nicht der Zahnschmerz in deinen Backen? ward dirs nicht dunkel vor den Augen?
sentences.l: did it not roar in your ears? did the toothache not gnaw in your cheeks? did it not grow dark before your eyes?
sentences.i: Was there not a roaring in your ears? Did the toothache not gnaw in your cheeks? Did it not go dark before your eyes?
sentences.n: dirs is dir es run together, and both clauses are impersonal, with nothing much for a subject: it roared for you, it grew dark for you. Backen here are cheeks, not baking.

sentences.t: Über das alles, hat nicht mein leiblicher Bruder, der Schlaf, dich jeden Abend an mich erinnert? lagst du nicht in der Nacht, als wärst du schon gestorben?“
sentences.l: Over and above all that, has not my own brother, Sleep, reminded you of me every evening? did you not lie at night as if you had already died?”
sentences.i: And over and above all that — has not my own brother, Sleep, reminded you of me every evening? Did you not lie at night as though you had already died?”
sentences.n: leiblicher Bruder is a brother of the same body, a full blood brother. Sleep as the brother of Death is far older than this tale, and the 1857 text simply assumes the reader knows it. wärst is the subjunctive after als: as if you had died.

sentences.t: Der Mensch wußte nichts zu erwiedern, ergab sich in sein Geschick und gieng mit dem Tode fort.
sentences.l: The man knew nothing to answer, gave himself over to his fate and went away with Death.
sentences.i: The man had nothing to answer; he resigned himself to his fate and went away with Death.
sentences.n: sich in sein Geschick ergeben is to resign oneself to one’s fate — Geschick here is destiny, not skill. gieng … fort, from fortgehen. There is no moral at the end: the tale stops where the argument does.

glossary.backen: der Backen — cheek, cheeks (dat. pl.; in deinen Backen, in your cheeks); not backen, to bake
glossary.befehlen: der Befehl — commands, orders (dat. pl.; meinen Befehlen gehorchen: to obey my orders)
glossary.bleibe: bleiben — I remain, I stay (1st sg. present; ‘liegen bleibe’ = stay lying)
glossary.boten: der Bote — messenger, messengers (acc. sg. and pl.; die Boten des Todes, the messengers of Death)
glossary.es: es — it; also the placeholder subject set in front of the verb (‘es stirbt niemand’ = nobody dies)
glossary.fremde: der Fremde — the stranger (masc. noun from the adjective fremd, strange, foreign)
glossary.geschick: das Geschick — fate, destiny (sich in sein Geschick ergeben: to resign oneself to one’s fate)
glossary.geschickt: schicken — sent (past participle, geschickt); not the adjective geschickt, skilful
glossary.richtete: aufrichten — raised up, set upright (3rd sg. past; separable, ‘richtete ihn auf’)
glossary.ringen: ringen — to wrestle, to struggle (infinitive; mit jemandem ringen)
glossary.schlaf: der Schlaf — sleep (the noun; here Death’s own brother)
glossary.trank: der Trank — draught, drink (acc. sg.; einen stärkenden Trank)
glossary.vertreten: vertreten — to bar, to block (infinitive; einem den Weg vertreten: to bar someone’s way)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (acc. sg.; einem den Weg vertreten: to bar someone’s way); elsewhere weg = away
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st sg. present: ‘daß ich weiß wann du kommst’ = that I know when you are coming); not weiß, white
glossary.werde: werden — shall, will (1st sg. present; ‘sterben werde ich nicht’ = I shall not die)
glossary.zog: ziehen — went on, journeyed (3rd sg. past; ‘zog weiter’ = travelled on); elsewhere to pull
glossary.überfallen: überfallen — to fall upon, to set upon (the über- is inseparable, so the infinitive and the past participle look alike; here the infinitive)
